# Agricultural Ecosystem Intelligence Daily Brief — 20 November 2026

**Prepared:** 20 November 2026 (Africa/Lagos)  
**Research window:** current public-source review available on 20 November 2026; selected background sources from earlier in 2026 are explicitly dated.  
**Purpose:** catch-up report after the scheduled 21:00 run produced no visible brief text. This is the report generated by the immediate replay, not the missing scheduled-run output.

## 1. Five-minute front brief

### Overall assessment

Today's strongest signal is a widening gap between **announced agricultural support and the details needed to act on it**. The federal government has announced fertiliser and grain interventions; Plateau has important potato infrastructure announcements; Nigeria has an evidenced cassava-starch import stream while industry reporting raises questions about local processor utilisation. None of these announcements or market signals yet gives us a confirmed low-capital commercial role.

### Five important developments

1. **Federal fertiliser and grain intervention.** On 20 November, FMAFS said three million bags of fertiliser were being prepared for release within the next month and stored grains under the Bank of Agriculture's Guaranteed Minimum Price programme would soon enter the market. Distribution modalities and grain quantities, grades, locations, prices and eligibility were not yet specified. This updates OPP-0002 and OPP-0003, but does not prove that a distributor or intermediary can participate. [EVD-0007]
2. **Wet-season output outlook is positive but not conclusive.** NAERLS reported that 13 of 17 assessed major crops are expected to record higher production in 2026. The assessment involved teams working across all 36 states and the FCT from 31 August to 6 September. It is a wet-season survey/outlook, not a final full-year production census; a separate dry-season assessment is planned. [EVD-0007]
3. **Plateau food inflation fell month-on-month.** October food inflation was -5.83% month-on-month in Plateau, while Nigeria's national food inflation was 19.13% year-on-year and -0.75% month-on-month. This is an index movement, not proof that every Plateau market price fell or that food is affordable. [EVD-0008]
4. **Plateau potato assets may be underused or not yet fully operational.** The state government reported a tissue-culture laboratory, potato processing facility, three processing plants, nine community markets and nine diffuse-light stores. A later media report describes the three plants as planned. The operating status, capacity, ownership, access terms and off-take need facility-level confirmation. [EVD-0009]
5. **Cassava offers two different value-chain investigations.** WITS records 3,227.65 tonnes of cassava-starch imports in 2025 worth about US$2.16 million, mostly from Thailand. Separately, ILRI documents conversion of cassava peels into high-quality feed ingredient. These are distinct routes: industrial starch supply versus by-product-to-feed processing. Neither is yet a validated local business. [EVD-0012; EVD-0013]

### Three strongest investigations (not validated opportunities)

| Rank | Investigation | Why it matters | Existing route / zero-capital view | Main uncertainty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Plateau potato facility utilisation (OPP-0007) | Local project assets may create needs around farmer access, seed multiplication, storage, processing, quality and market linkage. | Start with the project implementation office and existing operators; information/coordination may be low-capital only if authorised. | Which assets are operational and accessible now? |
| 2 | Cassava starch supply and processor utilisation (OPP-0005) | Recorded imports provide a real historical trade signal while domestic industry reports describe under-utilised capacity. | Map existing processors and industrial buyers before considering any build; a zero-capital introduction/data role is unproven. | Can local processors meet specifications and compete on landed cost? |
| 3 | Cassava peels-to-feed (OPP-0006) | An ILRI-described technology offers a route to turn a processing residue into a feed ingredient. | Reuse existing ILRI technology and identify existing processors/feed mills; coordination may be possible before buying equipment. | Local peel volume, safe processing cost and actual buyer demand. |

### Two things to watch

- Official implementation details for fertiliser release and grain distribution: participating firms, price, location, quantities, eligibility and procurement channels.
- Global rice, sugar and vegetable-oil balances: FAO expects tighter conditions in these markets even while wheat and coarse-grain supplies remain relatively comfortable.

### One practical action today

Use the published NASC and Plateau project contacts only to request information, not to commit money. The most valuable free first step for the new leads is to identify the responsible Plateau potato project office/operator and ask for a current facility-status note. No supplier contact or agency response is recorded as completed today.

### Something you might never have thought of

**Potato project assets as a service-discovery map.** The opportunity may not be to build another potato plant. It may be a missing service around existing assets: seed scheduling, farmer access, quality grading, storage booking, throughput coordination, packaging, buyer specifications or maintenance. This is a hypothesis; first verify that the facilities exist and can actually be used.

## 2. Full intelligence report

### 2.1 Production and agricultural resources

NAERLS' 2026 wet-season assessment points to increased output for 13 of 17 major crops, but the survey is not a final national production census and excludes the separate dry-season assessment. It identifies the need for better storage, post-harvest handling and market access so that higher output can translate into lower consumer prices. The national survey does not establish yields or production for each Plateau LGA. [EVD-0007]

NiMet's 2026 Seasonal Climate Prediction portal provides rainfall onset/cessation, seasonal length, rainfall amounts, temperature, dry-spell and crop-calendar information. The operational requirement is to check the relevant LGA forecasts against actual observed conditions; this brief does not claim an updated rainfall observation for every Plateau LGA. [Source: https://nimet.gov.ng/scp?id=15]

### 2.2 Commodity and product intelligence

New candidate products have been added to the working catalogue with distinct commercial forms:

- Roma tomato (fresh); layer day-old chicks; broiler finisher feed.
- Cassava starch (processed industrial ingredient); wet cassava peels (by-product); high-quality cassava peel mash/meal (processed feed ingredient).
- Maize grain; rice grain (with paddy and milled forms to be separated); fresh cassava roots.
- Cashew nuts in shell; standard-quality cocoa beans; sesame seeds.

The three export products are supported by reported Q2 2026 export-value analysis, not a current price quote or direct buyer demand. The top ten agricultural export categories were reported at ₦747.54 billion, with cashew nuts in shell, cocoa beans and sesame as the leading categories in the analysis. [EVD-0017]

The product catalogue remains open-ended. It is not limited to these candidates or the original 60 items.

### 2.3 Price and market intelligence

No L1 completed agricultural transaction was independently verified in today's review, and no new L2 identifiable direct seller quotation was confirmed.

Two market platforms provide signals, but their limitations matter:

- Agromate displays a Jos South Roma tomato listing for 1.5 tonnes at ₦450,000 per tonne (₦22,500 per basket of about 50 kg). The listing is explicitly marked pilot demonstration data and the seller's identity is not yet verified. Treat it as L3 platform data, not an order, live stock or a verified quotation. [EVD-0014]
- FarmPaddy displayed a Plateau estimate of ₦360,000 per 100 layer day-old chicks and a broiler finisher feed reference of ₦21,500 per 25 kg bag. The platform describes its values as estimates; there is no named seller, breed/batch, feed brand/formula or delivery term attached. Do not use these as procurement prices without direct confirmation. [EVD-0015]

The October CPI provides context rather than a substitute for market observations: Plateau food inflation was -5.83% month-on-month, while national food inflation remained 19.13% year-on-year. Household and market-level prices can move differently from the index. [EVD-0008]

**Price conclusion:** the price register should not be populated with any of these as verified transactions. Keep the market observation fields ready for identifiable quotations with date, market, unit, grade, quantity and terms.

### 2.4 Supply chain and distribution

The federal plan to release fertiliser and stored grains could affect input distribution, wholesale grain supply, storage and transport. At present, neither the fertiliser distribution map nor the grain release process has been published in enough detail to identify authorised distributors, release points, buyer rules or a permitted intermediary role. Continue OPP-0002 and OPP-0003 as verification tasks, not assumed commission opportunities. [EVD-0007]

For Plateau potato, the state project announcement identifies roads, markets and storage alongside seed and processing assets. Their current operating status and access terms determine whether this is a functioning supply chain or infrastructure still requiring commissioning, repair or operational arrangements. [EVD-0009]

### 2.5 Processing and industrial intelligence

**Cassava starch:** WITS/UN Comtrade records Nigerian cassava-starch imports of 3,227,650 kg in 2025, valued at US$2.160 million. Thailand supplied most of the reported quantity, followed by Turkey, China and India. This is a real historical import flow, but it does not prove that a buyer is currently seeking a new domestic supplier. [EVD-0012]

A November industry report describes domestic cassava processors as operating at about 15% of installed capacity and attributes the difficulty to cost, financing and competitiveness. Treat the capacity figure as secondary reporting pending processor-level confirmation. The central question is not simply “can we make starch?” It is whether existing plants can supply the right starch grade at a delivered cost that industrial users will accept. [EVD-0012]

**Cassava peels:** ILRI describes a technology that converts wet cassava peels into high-quality cassava peel mash/meal for animal feed. This is an existing technology to investigate, not an invention we need to recreate. The local chain requires fresh peel collection, safe and rapid processing, drying, quality control, feed formulation and an actual feed-mill buyer. No Plateau deployment was verified. [EVD-0013]

### 2.6 Trade, finance and investment

Q2 2026 agricultural export analysis points to cashew, cocoa and sesame as major Nigerian export-value categories. This supports continued discovery around export specifications, cleaning, sorting, traceability, aggregation and buyer requirements, but export values are not a proxy for farmer margins or easy entry into export trade. [EVD-0017]

Federal announcements also mention financing and investment programmes, including agricultural development finance and processing investment. No specific accessible financing facility, eligibility approval or capital commitment for the user's participation was verified today. [EVD-0007]

### 2.7 Global agricultural and agrifood intelligence

FAO's 19 November Food Outlook describes global supplies as generally comfortable for wheat and coarse grains, but tighter balances for rice, sugar and vegetable oils. It forecasts cereal stocks up 1.8% by the close of the 2027 seasons, world cereal trade down 3.3% in 2026/27, rice output declining for the first time in four seasons, and record oilseed production alongside stronger vegetable-oil demand from biofuels. FAO also expects moderate growth in global meat output led by poultry, while capture fisheries output faces pressure. [EVD-0011]

For Nigeria, the implications are conditional: global supply, freight, exchange rates, import exposure and local production all influence landed prices. Do not convert a global forecast into a Plateau price forecast without a transmission pathway.

### 2.8 Innovation and existing solutions

The most actionable solution discovery today is ILRI's cassava-peel feed technology. The project principle is to find existing processes, equipment providers and feed users before proposing any new build. For potatoes, the tissue-culture laboratory and processing facilities are existing public project assets to verify; the next innovation question is how to utilise what exists, not what new platform to build. [EVD-0013; EVD-0009]

### 2.10 Creative and unconventional problem-solving

Look for a **shared-use model** around potato facilities: if processors, stores or tissue-culture facilities are operational but underutilised, identify whether multiple cooperatives or buyers can book capacity, share logistics or aggregate inputs against processing runs. This may be cheaper than building parallel facilities. It remains a hypothesis pending operator confirmation, capacity data and access policy.

For cassava, investigate whether the same processor's residue stream can support feed production without interrupting the core starch/flour process. Avoid assuming that the residue is safe or valuable until quality and volume are measured.

### 2.11 Decision intelligence

The best next investigation is the Plateau potato project facility-status check because it is geographically close, has multiple publicly reported assets and could reveal several service gaps without initial inventory investment. Cassava starch is second because trade data is measurable, although competing on price may require substantial capital. HQCP ranks third because technical feasibility must be paired with local feed demand.

Do not buy stock, equipment or raw materials on the basis of today's public-source signals.

## 4. Coverage limits

Today's run used selected official, research-institution, trade, marketplace and media sources. It did not collect fresh direct farmgate/wholesale/retail quotations from every Plateau LGA, independently validate every platform listing, enumerate all processors or producers across all 36 states, or deeply assess every product family, fishery, livestock category, forest product, input or by-product. These are coverage gaps, not evidence that such markets or opportunities do not exist.
